item.title: Trump says DOJ will settle remaining Camp Lejeune claims if GOP wins midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What started as a disjointed speech in Greenville from President Donald Trump ended as a rallying cry from the president to elect struggling Republican candidates on North Carolina’s ballot. Trump went as far as to promise $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans take back the House and Senate — a promise he’s made in the past — and to also tie the election results to pending lawsuits by Marines who have suffered serious medical complications from contaminated water at Camp Lejeune. “Tonight, I’m pleased to announce that my administration has delivered $1 billion in cash settlements to these veterans and their families, most of whom are based here,” Trump said. Trump said if Republicans win the House and Senate he will direct the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible. “If we don’t win, there’s no money,” Trump said. “If we do win, you’re getting it." Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, immediately posted on social media in response to Trump’s statement. “Real leaders fight for the people, not for power,” Stein said. “To condition doing the right thing by sick North Carolinians on who wins the election is foul.” Andrew Bates, a former spokesman for President Joe Biden and an adviser to former Gov. Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign, called Trump’s statement “an anti patriotic thing for the president to say.” Boosting Whatley and bashing Cooper Trump, standing at Pitt-Greenville Airport, told the audience of around 1,500, according to pool reports, that he came to North Carolina for two reasons: “I want to tell you how bad Cooper is, and I want to tell you how great Michael Whatley is.” Cooper, 69, a Democrat from Raleigh, is running against Whatley, 58, a Republican from Gastonia. And Cooper has led every poll since the two men entered the race in July 2025, often by double digits. That’s led key national Republican groups to pull ad funding from Whatley’s campaign and invest in other candidates around the country. And as the rally was underway, news broke that the No Going Back PAC, a super PAC tied to Trump, pulled out of North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District race, Punchbowl News reported. Only North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, served by Rep. Don Davis, a Democrat from Snow Hill, had originally been expected to be a battleground, and Republican legislators redrew Davis’ district to favor a win for their party. Davis is running against former Trump adviser Laurie Buckhout, a Republican from Edenton. But with Trump’s job approval at an all-time low, and Whatley’s inability to raise his name recognition, despite having led both the state and national Republican parties, there’s been a trickle-down effect to at least five congressional districts among the state’s 14. And that includes the 11th Congressional District, where state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom added her name to the Republican ticket at the last hour after U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican from Flat Rock, withdrew from the race due to a sexual harassment scandal involving congressional employees. Whatley, Buckhout and Balkcom all spoke on stage both before and during Trump’s speech. The same day, the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics changed the 1st and 11th Congressional District ratings from “toss-up” races to “leans Democrat .” Both are in districts that typically are solidly Republican. Republicans hope to ramp up turnout Early Republican turnout was down compared to where it stood in 2022, the last midterm election, according to Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper. State Republican Party Chairman Jason Simmons kicked off Tuesday night’s rally by telling the audience to vote Republican up and down the ballot and to bring friends. “Make sure to go vote, but don’t go alone,” Simmons said. At least one person in the audience said she still hadn’t made up her mind, even about Trump. Maggie Lynn Heron-Heidel, who moved to Tarboro six months ago from Connecticut, write dystopian books and said “there are a lot of people who insist Trump is straight out of a dystopian novel.” She said she hadn’t made up her mind on Trump or his policies so she came to hear him speak. And some of her top concerns were rising costs, especially at the grocery store. Gas prices Trump didn’t address groceries but did talk about gas prices, which have risen as Trump continues a war he started against Iran to stop the country from having nuclear weapons. Trump said Tuesday night, “This is a very small price to pay for keeping a nuclear weapon away from the world’s number one state sponsor of terror.” He promised to lower gas prices again when the war ends. Glenn Mancher, a Merry Hill resident originally from Brooklyn, New York, drove an hour to attend Tuesday night’s rally, wearing a Trump 2028 hat. ”I’d like Trump to finish off the Iranians as quickly as possible,” Mancher said. “That would bring down energy prices.” Bates told McClatchy exclusively that Tuesday’s rally is a “visceral reminder of Michael Whatley’s support for the Iran War that’s making gas and diesel prices skyrocket.” “That’s on top of the unprecedented cuts to health care Whatley wanted, which are hurting people all over Eastern North Carolina just so billionaires like Elon Musk can pay lower taxes,” Bates said. He called Tuesday’s rally “just about the worst message you could take to the Old North State right now.” Crime Trump appeared in North Carolina just 34 days prior and called North Carolina cities “blood-soaked killed fields“ leaning into Republican messaging that Cooper was soft on crime because of the release of more than 3,500 prisoners during the COVID-19 pandemic under a legal settlement. Cooper and other North Carolina officials were sued by civil rights groups during the pandemic after Cooper refused to release half the state’s prison population. A judge told North Carolina officials he’d likely side with the civil rights groups and find that the prison conditions were no longer constitutional because of the virus. To prevent the release of 18,000 inmates, state officials say, they settled and released 3,500. They included DeCarlos Brown on the list of people who were released, despite Brown having already served his full sentence prior to the settlement being agreed upon. But in August 2025, after police said Brown killed Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on the light rail in Charlotte, Republicans have used the prison release against Cooper’s Senate campaign. On Tuesday, Trump called Cooper “a fool.” “He’s a super liberal fool,” Trump said. “I think a fool, because a senator who cares more about shielding murderers from a cough or a virus or something that will not — for the most part these killers were young, and instead of protecting innocent citizens from bloodthirsty killers — then Roy Cooper is the Dumocrat.” Trump signed into law the CARES Act passed by Congress that allowed the release of more than 13,000 federal prisoners into home confinement during the pandemic. Trump never brought up the CARES Act during Tuesday’s speech but said “it’s crazy” Cooper could become senator after abiding by the court settlement. He and Whatley also questioned Cooper’s mental acuity, a new line of attack from Republicans against Cooper after The North State Journal published a cease-and-desist demand from the Cooper campaign in response to a reporter from the outlet questioning whether he had a “neurological issue.” Cooper’s lawyers said Cooper does not, and that to publish anything to the contrary would be defamatory. Trump turned his attention to Whatley, crediting him for the success of Trump’s 2024 campaign. At the time, Whatley was leading the Republican National Committee. “A lot of people said it’s one of the best campaigns ever run,” Trump said. “I wanted him to be the guy, and I was right. I called it right. And I think he’ll be an even better senator.” Trump handpicked Whatley to succeed Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from Huntersville, who got into a public feud with Trump over how Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill would affect North Carolina’s Medicaid recipients. That caused Tillis to drop his reelection bid, and Trump to tap Whatley to run against Cooper. Trump’s visit Tuesday night came one day after the vice president traveled to Hendersonville for a similar rally, and exactly two weeks before the election. Trump said he will likely come to the state again before Nov. 3. This article originally appeared on Raleigh News and Observer at https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article317709089.html

item.title: Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, sources say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week. Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine. It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed. Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X . Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order. The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications. Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown. "I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service. "We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success." Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service. What is Starshield? Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink. The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close. What happened in Ukraine? Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable. Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes. Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones. The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things." Zelensky has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored." The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week. "There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend . Why have Trump and Zelensky clashed? Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelensky has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S. , and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine." Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week. Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/elon-musk-ukraine-spacex-starshield-trump-administration/

item.title: Trump says the economy is booming. Vance says there's more work to do.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Bill Clinton famously said he could feel voters’ pain over the economy. But these days, when it comes to questions about high prices , President Donald Trump insists that the pain is his. “They hit me with affordability, and that’s the first time I ever heard the word used,” he complained in Nebraska earlier this month. The White House leaves Vice President JD Vance to use a softer touch. Last month in Texas, he admitted “there are people out there who are frustrated by the pace of progress." And during a CBS News town hall on Saturday, Vance said, “I recognize that gas prices are too high right now" and "we’re working on it.” Depending on which Republican is speaking, Americans are getting a different perspective on how bad things are with the economy. Trump says “the golden age of America is upon us.” Vance walks a tightrope to show that he knows voters are feeling an economic pinch while still selling them on Trump's agenda. The disconnect comes as Americans’ confidence in the economy sank to the lowest level in more than a decade this month, the average long-term U.S. mortgage rate jumped this month to its highest level in nearly three years and the unemployment rate ticked up last month . Recent economic data released this month shows that high gasoline prices are intensifying inflation and more expensive oil and gas have begun to push prices up in other parts of the economy. While most of Trump's supporters don't hold him at fault, some acknowledge that the president's penchant for salesmanship may not hit the mark. "I think he talks it up,” said Conda Little, a 76-year-old retiree who went to see Trump in Dalton, Georgia, on Friday. “I think Vance is more real.” Little takes the president at his word that he will achieve a victory over Iran in a way that benefits U.S. consumers back home. But she said it’s impossible to deny the fallout from the conflict. “Everybody’s real upset about the gas” and “groceries are out of sight,” she said. “It’s hard. It’s really hard,” she said, adding that, “I think that people need to hear the truth.” ‘We need to do more’ Trump is loath to acknowledge concerns. He told reporters earlier this month that he gives himself “an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything.” He has dismissed concerns about high costs, arguing that concerns about affordability are a “hoax.” “We’re in the golden age of America. So our nation is doing better now than ever before,” he told a crowd in Kentucky on Saturday while campaigning for Republican candidates. Trump has occasionally acknowledged that gas prices are high , but has called it “a small price to pay” for keeping the country and the world safe with the Iran war. Trump’s discordant message with one of the top concerns voters are voicing ahead of the midterm elections has seemed heightened by his fixation on beautifying Washington and building a large ballroom at the White House. During a visit this month to an economically struggling corner of Arizona, he regaled the crowd with the story about how he ended up with a luxury jet gifted by Qatar to use as Air Force One. Vance, as he crisscrosses the country, is quick to say that the administration has more work to do. To cast blame, the vice president often says that his administration’s Democratic predecessors put the country in such a deep hole that they need more time to climb out. To show empathy, he often references his own experience growing up in a working-class family in a Rust Belt town. That's far different from Trump, who comes from a wealthy family, is a billionaire and even joked during his speeches on Friday and Saturday that if people have lunch at his Mar-a-Lago club, "for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert.” Vance, during a CBS News town hall that aired on Saturday, said: “I grew up in a working-class family. When gas prices were high, I know that it made my grandmother suffer, and I’m sure that you’re struggling with it in a variety of ways." When asked by the moderator about the mixed message he and Trump are giving on the economy, Vance said Trump was speaking about new investments coming into the country, but said the changes take time. “We need to do more, and we can certainly do better,” he acknowledged. Many Trump supporters trust his pitch Some voters said Trump’s rosy view on the economy turns them away, like Santiago Rodriguez, a 19-year-old Texas college student who will be voting for the first time this year. Rodriguez, who attended a campaign rally last week for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, said he would consider voting for a Republican but not while Trump is in charge because he doesn’t grasp the high cost of living for Americans. “I think he’s out of touch, I think he’s never seen what a true day as a Texan or anybody in general who is in the working class,” Rodriguez said. Trump's most loyal supporters aren’t interested in blaming high prices on anything the president has done. Cindy Massengill, a 67-year-old who came to see Trump in Dalton, Georgia, said she felt he’s doing the best he can. “I’m positive that he’s got done more than any other president after the mess we were left with Obama and Biden,” she said. Mary Bunker, a 67-year-old Republican who attended Trump’s Monday rally near Wichita, Kansas, said she works multiple jobs, including as a waitress and DoorDash driver. She feels the pressure of high gas prices, but she likes the tax breaks that Trump signed into law last year and she doesn’t fault the way he speaks about economic concerns. “I think he’s a very good businessman,” Bunker said. “He’s been in business a long time, so I think he knows what he’s talking about.” ___ Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Dalton, Georgia, Jesse Bedayn in San Marcos, Texas, and Nicholas Ingram in Park City, Kansas, contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/golden-age-vs-were-working-040104930.html

item.title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found. The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S. Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters. "What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating." The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people , all of them green card holders , on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote. As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections. "HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders." Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities. "In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident of initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations. In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering. Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN , describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms , approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS." One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand. The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment. For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters. "It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University. "And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that — because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth." A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear." "Target List" In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, " Target List ." That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS. In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject. DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters. "Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally," said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ." "There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden. She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/federal-agents-seek-noncitizen-voters/

item.title: Elon Musk wants to combine Tesla and SpaceX. But would investors benefit?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Joe Brock Oct 21 (Reuters) - Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create one of the most valuable companies in the world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company SpaceX ‌were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, satellite communications, and ‌computing infrastructure, including data centers on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: WHY WOULD MUSK DO THIS? A merger would create a single company at the center of Musk's long-term vision: an ​integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centers), connectivity," Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing the companies together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Musk's projects already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. ‌A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy ⁠capital, engineering talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate ⁠his influence. WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR INVESTORS? Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in ​automobiles, ​robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined ​company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly ‌interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. WHERE COULD SPACEX AND TESLA WORK TOGETHER? Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future data-center projects. Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-center ambitions. Musk hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale ‌factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialize Starship production, while SpaceX technologies have already appeared in ​Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could ​also coordinate efforts to secure strategic supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, ​semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialized metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite hardware. WHAT ARE THE DOWNSIDE RISKS? The biggest challenges ‌may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US ​military, intelligence agencies and NASA. Tesla, meanwhile, ​remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors would need to be persuaded that combining ​two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them ‌separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centers, ​mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place ​them under one roof. (Reporting by Joe Brock; Editing by Peter Henderson and Sonali Paul) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/explainer-why-musk-merge-spacex-020904506.html

item.title: Kagan accuses Supreme Court's conservative majority of undermining democracy
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Justice Elena Kagan spoke at Catholic University of America in Washington on Tuesday. (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty) WASHINGTON — Liberal Justice Elena Kagan sharply criticized the Supreme Court’s conservative majority Tuesday, saying it undermined democracy in a series of rulings, including several that have prompted a new wave of legislative map-drawing that has increasingly eliminated competitive districts . Kagan, who has dissented in those cases, also took aim at the majority for striking down campaign finance restrictions and, as she put it, the “evisceration” of the landmark 1965 Voting Rights Act that was enacted to protect minority voters. “Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions,” she said in remarks at Catholic University’s law school in Washington, D.C. “I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should,” she added. Kagan was referring in particular to the 2019 ruling that said federal courts could not intervene to limit extreme partisan gerrymandering. She also mentioned a series of rulings that have gutted the Voting Rights Act, including one this year that led to Republican states eliminating majority Black districts. The court has also consistently struck down campaign finance restrictions, the most recent in June. Heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, several states have redrawn their congressional maps to maximize the number of seats the majority party can win in that state. Texas kicked things off, at President Donald Trump’s urging, followed by other states, including California. The 2019 redistricting ruling has been particularly harmful, Kagan said. As a result, “both parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders.” The lopsided maps deny people “their rights to voting equality” and have the effect of “driving people away from the center, towards the wings, toward the extremes” because candidates only have to worry about winning the primary, she added. The failure of the court to take action on the issue is “making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” Kagan said. When states draw legislative districts that almost wipe out the ability of many voters to elect their chosen candidate, it is “very destructive of our democracy,” she added. As for the increasingly unlimited amounts of money in politics, Kagan said that many voters find it disconcerting. “I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she said. During the question-and-answer session with professor Joel Alicea, Kagan was also critical of the Supreme Court’s ruling this year that gave Trump greater control over hitherto independent federal agencies that were set up by Congress to be free from political interference. She questioned the wisdom of giving the president too much power, saying there is a “danger of one president being able to ride roughshod over all the other institutions of government and over the people.” But Kagan also defended the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, over claims from the left that it is a rubber stamp for Trump. She cited several rulings in which the president lost, including his attempt to impose sweeping tariffs. The court is “deeply conservative,” she said, but in certain cases “definitely pushed back on the president.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/justice-elena-kagan-accuses-conservative-majority-undermining-democrac-rcna604673

item.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Monday's lawsuit filed by "Jane Doe" alleges that a member of Alpha Delta Phi sexually assaulted her during a fraternity party on Feb. 7. (E. Jason Wambsgans / Chicago Tribune via Getty) A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses. The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants. “The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.” Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago. The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation. “These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.” Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.” “The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.” Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization. Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university. Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit. She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.” “I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.” She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.” The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says. The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances. “I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News. The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says. After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her. Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on. She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night. The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report. Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report. Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit. A spokesperson for the city’s police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department’s involvement in the case. Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs. Doe’s lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also “ensure that this doesn’t happen again, and to help reform” policies within the university. The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case. “At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it’s not rare. It happens way more than people realize,” Doe said. “There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/woman-sexually-assaulted-fraternity-university-chicago-lawsuit-alleges-rcna604607

item.title: The Villages bets $180 million on Florida retirees as home sales slump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Villages, the largest retirement community in the US with roughly 170,000 residents across 57,000 acres in central Florida, is aiming to get even bigger. The resort-like community plans to issue $180 million in high-yield debt primarily to finance more homes, according to an investor presentation this week. The proceeds of the upcoming bond offering will fund construction of 3,860 new residential units and additional golf courses and recreation centers, according to Bloomberg . The community is already massive, with more than 50 golf courses, 100-plus swimming pools, and several town squares, and its latest expansion bets big on luring droves of more boomers and Gen Xers to the Sunshine State. But it's happening as the bond market is under duress , with even the mighty US Treasury market competing for investors. The housing market is grounded by high mortgage rates and high home prices. Florida has been hit particularly hard by the trends. Sales of existing single-family homes there were down 3.5% in September from a year ago, according to the Florida Realtors Association. And net migration into the state slowed sharply last year compared to the pandemic boom years. What's more: The notion of what makes an ideal retirement community is evolving. "The retirement relocation conversation in this country has been dominated by weather, taxes, and cost of living for decades," demographic strategist Bradley Schurman told Yahoo Finance. "Those are real factors, but they tell you almost nothing about whether a place will remain livable and financially viable over the 25 years that matter most to a new retiree." If they build it, will they come? The Villages taps into several essential keys to healthy aging — community and social engagement, along with a focus on fitness and recreation. Its expansion plans would have around 260,000 people living there with more than 130,000 homes by 2045. So far this year, more than 2,100 homes in the Villages have sold for an average of just under $500,000, per Bloomberg. "There's still juice in these master planned communities like the Villages, and there's a market for them," Schurman said. But while the Villages has been a colossal draw for retirees seeking warm weather, low taxes, and a low cost of living, more factors related to affordability and sustainability have entered the conversation. An index released earlier this year ranked communities on climate resilience, automation readiness, social cohesion, population renewal, and governance and foresight. For example, if an area's population is stable or growing, basic government services are more likely to be funded. Many of the places millions of Americans have been lured to in the past ranked at or near the bottom of this index. New York City ranked No. 1. The Villages was dead last. Low taxes are only one piece of the puzzle Cost of living is always top of mind for retirees, and in an era of high inflation, that category is expanding. Yes, there are housing costs and taxes, but also utility bills, insurance, healthcare costs, gasoline, and groceries. Medicare premiums, which vary considerably by market, are also in their calculator. Climate change and disaster risk can't be ignored. The utility costs of running air-conditioning in southern retirement spots like Florida and Arizona may make these places less appealing. Homeowner and storm insurance costs are soaring and show little sign of easing. Many people choose a retirement locale with zero income tax — a critical factor — but you've also got to account for state and local taxes, which can reach 7% or more. Florida, for example, imposes no state income tax, no Social Security taxes, no inheritance tax, no estate tax, and no taxes on retirement income such as pensions, IRAs, or 401(k)s. But it has significant sales taxes and property taxes. Another consideration Schurman noted: If you have kids or family you want to transfer your wealth to, and your retirement home is an asset, the question for Villages residents is "are these assets turning into liabilities for the homeowner?" "If a chunk of your wealth is tied up in a resort property that might be in a riskier climate zone, and also where selling might be difficult in the coming years because you're going to have a very limited audience of people who would actually purchase from you when there's newer housing available, you need to pay attention," he said. Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich." item.title: Trump administration says it has revoked over 300,000 visas as crackdown escalates
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Kanishka Singh WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration has revoked over 300,000 US visas during his second term, the ‌State Department said on Tuesday as the federal government continues its ‌sweeping immigration crackdown. The number showed an acceleration in the pace of visa revocations in recent ​weeks. In an update issued on August 10, the State Department had put the number of visa revocations since Trump's current term began in January 2025 at over 175,000. Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to improve ‌domestic security. Rights advocates ⁠say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ⁠ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling. In announcing the latest number on X, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the Trump administration "has revoked more ​visas at ​a faster pace than any administration ​in history." Pigott said the administration ‌had "zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law, commit fraud, or undermine our national security." Among visa revocations particularly condemned by rights advocates are those of pro-Palestinian foreign protesters demonstrating against US ally Israel's attacks on Gaza and of foreigners over their social media comments about conservative ‌commentator Charlie Kirk's assassination. In addition to attempts ​to deport foreign protesters, the Trump administration has ​enforced tightened social media screening ​of immigrants and visa applicants. Rights advocates say the government ‌has deployed national security reasons to ​target critics and ​used isolated cases of fraud to broadly target immigrant communities such as the Somali American community in Minnesota. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on ​stopping illegal immigration, his ‌administration has also made legal immigration more difficult — for example ​by imposing expensive fees for certain work visas. (Reporting by Kanishka Singh ​in Washington; Editing by Nia Williams) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/trump-administration-says-revoked-over-220518005.html

item.title: Trump administration freezes another $1.2 billion in California Medicaid payments
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator, speaks Tuesday in the Oval Office as President Trump and Nick Shirley listen. (Jacquelyn Martin / Associated Press) The Trump administration is deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to California, citing concerns about potential fraud in a state program that helps older adults and people with disabilities with everyday tasks. Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said federal officials took action after they grew concerned about the rapid expansion of California’s personal care services program in recent years. State officials were notified of the decision Tuesday, he said. “California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country,” Oz said. “Impossible for us to understand how that could be so we are taking major action in California.” Oz did not provide any evidence of fraud but suggested the state was paying people too much taxpayer money to help with services that could be offered for free, like “paying somebody to carry groceries upstairs for your mom.” “Many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, but in California, they will pay you a lot of money for it,” he said. Read more: Vance says $1.3 billion in Medicaid payments to California will be deferred over fraud concerns The move is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to withhold federal money from California. In May, the administration held back $1.3 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to the state over concerns about “fraudsters” in the state’s hospice and in-home care programs. The actions have been part of a broad effort by the administration to rein in fraud in federal healthcare benefits programs, particularly in Democrat-led states. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla criticized the administration’s decision. “This Administration’s track record speaks for itself: Fewer people have health insurance, premiums are up, and drug costs are higher. This decision will hurt older Californians, people with disabilities, and those recovering from illness or injury,” Padilla said in a statement. “The American people deserve better, and I’ll keep fighting against their attacks.” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the office has been critical of the administration’s past efforts. In May, Newsom’s office called the action to withhold funds for in-home care programs a “sick” and politically motivated attack on services that are meant to “keep seniors and people with disabilities OUT of nursing homes.” Those services usually cover assistants who help people with daily tasks such as bathing, laundry or cooking. They also provide needed care such as injections under the direction of a medical professional. A 2020 report by the California state auditor found that nearly three-quarters of In-home Supportive Services caregivers assist a family member. Newsom’s office, however, has argued that the program saves taxpayers money, saying IHSS care costs $30,000 a year, while nursing home care costs $137,000 a year. Read more: Medicaid reckoning awaits next California governor after program’s rapid expansion California’s hospice industry has had problems in the past and authorities have tried to crack down on the issue. A Times investigation in 2020 found that providers were billing Medicare for hospice services and equipment for patients who were not actually dying while the industry boomed. The Trump administration, led by Vice President JD Vance, has tried to focus attention on the issue of waste, fraud and abuse as a centerpiece policy platform to bring down healthcare costs. On Tuesday, Trump and Vance announced a $25-million whistleblower program designed to pay out cash to people who tip off the federal government about fraudsters. The program will offer a 1% commission for tips that lead to a successful conviction. Trump said he would be the sole arbitrator of who gets to keep the money. “I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous believe me. We are not looking to save on that,” Trump said. “I promise you I will be fair.” Trump said the money will be handed out “expeditiously and fairly.” “I promise there is nothing in this for me,” he said. The White House referred comment about the decision to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The federal agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Get the L.A. Times California Politics newsletter. Deeply reported insights into legislation, politics and policy from Sacramento, Washington and beyond, in your inbox twice per week. item.title: At least 9 more lawmakers say they were targets of suspicious mail
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said Tuesday that one of her district offices was mailed a suspicious envelope. Pool Photo by Adam Gray/UPI Oct. 21 (UPI) -- At least nine U.S. lawmakers announced Tuesday that suspicious envelopes had been mailed to their offices, the latest in a wave of similar mailings targeting federal legislators from both parties in the past week. More than three dozen senators and House members have reported receiving suspicious envelopes, some containing white powder or unknown substances, or having them intercepted by postal investigators. The mailings were first reported Oct. 13, when suspicious letters were received by the offices of elected officials in Louisiana and Oklahoma. On Tuesday, lawmakers who announced letters had been sent to their offices included Reps. Nanette Barragán, D-Calif.; Shontel Brown, D-Ohio; Jim Costa, D-Calif.; Robert Garcia, D-Calif.; Pablo José Hernández, D-P.R.; Donald Norcross, D-N.J.; and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.; and Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind.; and Deb Fischer, R-Neb. "This string of suspicious mailings started two weeks before a consequential midterm election and is seemingly intended to intimidate public servants and sow further division," Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement Tuesday, announcing that a suspicious letter had been delivered to her district office in Hunts Point. "Political violence has no place in our country. It is always unacceptable and we must all refuse to normalize an unsafe and volatile political environment where everyday people are put at risk." Pictures of the letters posted online by some lawmakers in the past week show that the intended recipients' names and addresses are handwritten, while the return addresses are printed and in some cases identical: a New York City address formerly used by the Democratic Socialists of America, a political organization that has denied involvement with the letters. There have been no reported injuries and federal and local authorities are investigating. No arrests have been announced. On Monday, House Sergeant at Arms William McFarland sent lawmakers a memo obtained by Roll Call stating, "none of the letters received by congressional offices have been determined to contain hazardous substances," but that more offices could receive similar letters "in the coming days." That same day, more than a dozen lawmakers said suspicious letters had been sent to their offices. "A single threat against one elected official is chilling enough. But it's more common than ever that elected officials and their staff -- no matter their title nor party -- are being targeted for no other reason than choosing public service," Norcross said in a statement Tuesday, announced that a suspicious envelope addressed to his Cherry Hill district office had been intercepted by postal service investigators a day prior. "That's unsustainable for any version of a healthy, functional government." item.title: Ramaswamy faces growing criticism over ad featuring Ohio rival's estranged mom
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A chorus of condemnation from some Ohio politicians is growing against Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over an attack ad produced by his campaign that featured his opponent's estranged mother criticizing her and questioning the years of abuse she endured as a child. The ad, which has not been aired on television but spread on social media, shows Dr. Amy Acton's estranged mother, Donna Stearns Arthur, criticizing Acton, calling her a liar and casting doubt on Acton's upbringing. Acton has been estranged from Arthur since 1978 when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, faced a rape charge for sexually assaulting Acton when she was 12 years old. Cledith died in southern Pennsylvania and was never convicted of the charge, and Acton's mother stayed married to him until his death. A clip of the ad, which blogger The Rooster shared on social media on Oct. 19 , shows Arthur accusing her daughter of lying about Acton's upbringing, which included homelessness, neglect and abuse, and urging Ohioans not to vote for Acton. "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem," Arthur says in the ad. "She is a liar. She lies about her past." Acton's brother, Phillip Stearns, condemned the ad, and said Ramaswamy "stooped to a despicable low" in attempting to turn Acton's abuse into a "political talking point." “After [Cledith] was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died," Stearns said of Arthur. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants." The Acton campaign released an ad later Oct. 20 of Acton's brother berating Ramaswamy over the ad, and saying that "Amy took the brunt of [the abuse]." More: Amy Acton’s brother slams ad featuring estranged mother Acton told WOSU that her mother is the one lying. "It's awful to see her this way, and it's even more incredible to see that my opponent [Ramaswamy] has taken advantage of someone who's clearly not well, who is older, and this is totally in line with who he is," Acton told WOSU. Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, doubled down on support for the ad and accused Acton of being a "serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor." Ramaswamy later Oct. 20 acknowledged to the USA TODAY Ohio Statehouse Bureau that his campaign produced the ad. "Her mother has spoken out for years and I don't know Amy Acton's mother and I've never met Amy Acton either," Ramaswamy said. "What I do know is that Amy Acton has been repeatedly and serially dishonest during this campaign and for much of her record in public service and I do believe that that record deserves to be scrutinized." Several prominent Democrats – including State Rep. Allison Russo, D-Upper Arlington, who is running for Ohio Secretary of State, and Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell, who is running for state auditor against Secretary of State Frank LaRose – called on Ohio Republicans in an Oct. 20 media release to condemn the ad, calling it a "new and unacceptable low in Ohio politics." "Every single Republican candidate running for statewide office should immediately and publicly denounce this ad," Russo and other Democrats said in the media release "Silence in the face of such destructive rhetoric is an endorsement of it. It is time to raise the standard of public discourse in Ohio and focus on the practical solutions our citizens deserve." David Axelrod, a political consultant and CNN analyst, also took to X to condemn Ramaswamy and said that he had an "unquenchable ambition" to become Ohio's next governor. "I've been around politics longer than [Ramaswamy's] been alive, and I don't think I've seen anything uglier," Axelrod wrote. Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, doubled down on support for the ad and accused Acton of being a "serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor." I'm not going to share this ad, in which @VivekGRamaswamy unconscionably mines @amyactonoh's family tragedy to advance his unquenchable ambition to become governor of OH.I've been around politics longer than he's been alive, and I don't think I've ever seen anything uglier. — David Axelrod (@davidaxelrod) October 20, 2026 The growing condemnation from both Democrats and some Republicans is part of the larger conversations swirling around campaign ads in Ohio. Campaigns have spent more than $450 million on ads, according to AdImpact, and have become more inflammatory and exaggerated as the respective races drag on. Jerry Miller, a professor of communication studies at Ohio University and an expert in political communications, told The Dispatch that while campaign advertising may appear especially combative this election season, its underlying purpose remains largely unchanged: to draw sharp contrasts, undermine opponents and shape voters' perceptions. Miller said that dynamic is particularly evident in the contest between Ramaswamy and Acton, neither of whom has previously held elected office. As a result, he said, campaign attacks are more likely to focus on questions of credibility, character and public image rather than records in elected office. Although the ad never formally aired on television, Miller said it still served multiple strategic purposes. On one hand, it sought to discredit Amy Acton; on the other, it initially provided Ramaswamy with a measure of plausible deniability because it was circulated on social media. Miller said the ad's online circulation may have been intentional, arguing that the attention generated by its release, including coverage from national media outlets such as the New York Times and ABC News has helped amplify its message and spark public discussion even without a traditional television rollout. "What is especially troubling with this ad is the subject matter and its use of a woman, presumably Amy Acton's mother, to deliver the allegations," Miller said in an email to The Dispatch. "Whether or not the ad was ever meant to air in major media markets, the attention it draws, from news outlets that cover it to scholars like me who study political advertising and communication, lends it a measure of legitimacy and widens its audience," he said. "That makes it a strategically effective move for whoever is behind it." Director of Ohio Department of Development says 'there are lines we shouldn't cross' Lydia Mihalik, director of the Ohio Department of Development, said the ad crossed lines that shouldn't have been crossed. item.title: Alabama governor spares death row inmate after doubts grow over murder conviction
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey on Tuesday commuted the death sentence of a death-row inmate after a number of former public officials and the current district attorney raised doubts about his conviction. The Republican governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson's death sentence to life in prison without parole. Johnson was convicted of the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. Johnson has long maintained he is innocent. "When presented with Mr. Johnson's case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death," Ivey said in a statement. "My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole." Ivey has overseen 27 executions during her time as governor. She has commuted the death sentences of three death-row inmates. Prior to the commutation, Ivey said she notified Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and a designated member of Hardy's family, Beverly Hardy, of her decision. "Capital punishment is too important of a tool for Alabama to not approach it carefully and seriously," Ivey added in her statement. "Mr. Johnson will serve the remainder of his life behind bars for the senseless murder of Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. No doubt, he is paying the price." Hardy was shot twice in the head while working off-duty security at a hotel. Johnson has maintained he was on the other side of town at the time of the shooting. Ty Alper, one of Toforest Johnson's attorneys, said they are grateful to Ivey for "diligently reviewing Toforest's case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution." Alper said the fight to overturn the conviction will continue. "Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family," Alper said. There has been a long-running legal effort to win a new trial in the case that has garnered national attention and was the subject of a podcast . Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr, who was elected in 2018, has supported Johnson's bid for a new trial. Carr wrote in a 2024 court filing that the "evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years." Carr said in 2024 that credible alibi witnesses place Johnson elsewhere at the time of the crime. He said there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness, a woman who "claimed she overheard Johnson confess to the murder on a three-way phone call on which she was eavesdropping." The key prosecution witness at Johnson's 1998 trial testified that, while eavesdropping on a phone call, she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the crime. She was paid $5,000 in 2001 for her testimony, and Johnson's lawyers argue that the state withheld evidence of monetary motivation for the testimony. A number of former judges and prosecutors have joined those seeking a new trial for Johnson amid questions about his conviction more than 20 years ago. Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, former Chief Justices Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers, and several former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials supporting a new trial.
